questions.q: What three pieces make up the DIY monitoring pattern described in this lesson?
options: A permanent logging table, a stored procedure that inserts a DMV snapshot into it, and a SQL Server Agent job that calls the procedure on a schedule
A linked server, a CLR assembly, and a Windows service
A third-party dashboard, a license key, and a support contract
A single ad-hoc query run manually whenever someone remembers to
questions.explain: The lesson builds the pattern from a logging table, a capture procedure, and a recurring Agent job — the same free building blocks used throughout this chapter.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, how often is the capture procedure scheduled to run via the Agent job?
options: Every 15 minutes
Once a year
Only when a user files a complaint
Every time the server restarts, and never again
questions.explain: The lesson uses the same 15-minute recurring capture interval introduced in the monitoring baseline lesson, wired up as an Agent job step.

questions.q: Why does the lesson include a retention cleanup job (deleting rows older than 60 days) alongside the capture job?
options: Without pruning, the logging table only ever grows, and can become its own performance problem over time
SQL Server requires all tables to be emptied every 60 days by law
Retention has nothing to do with performance and is purely cosmetic
60-day-old rows are automatically corrupted
questions.explain: A table that never has rows removed grows without bound; the retention job balances keeping enough history against unconstrained table growth.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect DIY monitoring scripts back to T-SQL for Database Administrators?
options: It extends that course's troubleshooting-toolkit idea — your own understood scripts — into something that runs continuously rather than only during an active incident
It replaces everything from that course with a commercial product
It claims T-SQL for Database Administrators covered Agent jobs in full depth already
There is no real connection; the reference is purely stylistic
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly builds on the toolkit concept from T-SQL for Database Administrators, turning reactive scripts into a continuously running, scheduled version of the same idea.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the real payoff of a DIY monitoring setup, beyond just logging data?
options: Actually reviewing the logged data — such as a weekly comparison, or wiring a baseline-comparison alert to the table — rather than letting it sit unused
The logging table itself, regardless of whether anyone ever queries it
Replacing SQL Server Agent with a third-party scheduler
Guaranteeing zero performance problems going forward
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that a logging table sitting untouched is no better than the raw DMVs it snapshots — the value comes from actually reviewing or alerting on the data.
